content: Jaundice is characterized by a yellowish discoloration of the skin, the conjunctiva (the clear membrane covering the sclera or whites of the eyes), and mucous membranes. This discoloration is caused by hyperbilirubinemia, which refers to elevated levels of bilirubin in the blood. For jaundice to become visibly apparent, the bilirubin concentration in the blood typically needs to exceed 2–3 mg/dL. The term jaundice originates from the French word jaune, meaning yellow. Historically, it was mistakenly believed that individuals with jaundice perceived everything as yellow, but this is not true. In 1885, Luhrman identified jaundice as a potential adverse effect of vaccination. Later, in 1935, the American surgeon A.O. Whipple first described obstructive jaundice. Between 1950 and 2000, many of the viruses responsible for hepatitis and jaundice were discovered. Jaundice is classified into two main categories: unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from increased bilirubin production, reduced hepatic uptake, or defects in bilirubin conjugation. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, on the other hand, is further subdivided into conditions such as biliary tract obstruction, intrahepatic cholestasis, hepatocellular parenchymal injury, and defects in hepatocellular canalicular excretion or sinusoidal reuptake. Bilirubin is a byproduct of the breakdown of heme, a component of red blood cells. It is primarily processed in the liver and spleen before undergoing metabolism, which involves hepatic uptake, conjugation, clearance, and excretion into bile. Jaundice occurs when bilirubin levels increase and accumulate in tissues, leading to the characteristic yellow discoloration. In neonates, jaundice can result from physiological bilirubin accumulation or pathological mechanisms. Pathological neonatal jaundice may be acquired (e.g., Rh hemolytic disease, ABO incompatibility, or G6PD deficiency) or inherited (e.g., Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome types I and II, Lucey-Driscoll syndrome, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, and Rotor syndrome). The causes of jaundice are broadly categorized into those associated with unconjugated and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia results from increased bilirubin production, impaired hepatic uptake, or defective conjugation, leading to an accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, however, is caused by intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholestasis, which leads to the buildup of conjugated bilirubin. The incidence of jaundice is approximately 40,000 cases per 100,000 intensive care unit patients. Neonatal jaundice is more prevalent among Asian and mixed Asian/white infants compared to white infants. Hepatocellular jaundice, often caused by viral hepatitis, is more common in younger individuals, while cholestatic jaundice, frequently associated with liver cancer, hepatitis, or cirrhosis, is more common in older adults. Men are more likely to develop hepatocellular jaundice and liver cancer, whereas women are more frequently affected by hemolytic jaundice, often due to cholangiocarcinoma. Risk factors for jaundice differ based on the type of hyperbilirubinemia. For unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, common risk factors include the neonatal period, certain medications (e.g., rifampin, probenecid), genetic syndromes (e.g., Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome types I and II), steroid use, and chronic liver diseases. For conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, risk factors include viral hepatitis, alcohol use, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, chronic hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, certain drugs and toxins (e.g., alkylated steroids, chlorpromazine, herbal medications, arsenic), sepsis, hypoperfusion states, infiltrative diseases (e.g., amyloidosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), pregnancy, cirrhosis, choledocholithiasis, biliary tract tumors, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and pancreatitis. Routine screening for jaundice is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. The natural history of jaundice varies widely depending on the underlying cause. Some individuals may recover fully without complications, while for others, jaundice may signal a life-threatening condition. The gold standard diagnostic test for jaundice is measuring plasma bilirubin levels. A bilirubin concentration exceeding 2–3 mg/dL is typically required for visible discoloration. Patients with jaundice may report symptoms such as yellowing of the skin, nausea, vomiting, fever, anorexia, dark urine, fatigue, pruritus, and right upper quadrant pain. A thorough history, including alcohol use, blood transfusions, viral hepatitis, and family history of liver disease, is essential. Physical examination findings in jaundice depend on the underlying cause and may include cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and peripheral edema. Laboratory findings reveal elevated serum total bilirubin levels, which can be categorized as conjugated or unconjugated. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is indicated by a serum conjugated bilirubin concentration >0.4 mg/dL, while unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is characterized by a conjugated bilirubin concentration <0.4 mg/dL. Imaging studies can aid in diagnosing the underlying cause of jaundice. Abdominal CT and MRI scans may reveal findings suggestive of cirrhosis, such as liver shrinkage, portal vein dilation, esophageal varices, splenomegaly, and ascites. Ultrasonography can also identify features of cirrhosis, including splenomegaly, ascites, and portal hypertension. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is another imaging modality used to diagnose cholestasis. Liver biopsy, though rarely necessary, remains the gold standard for diagnosing cirrhosis-related jaundice. Treatment for jaundice focuses on addressing the underlying cause. For example, viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, or cirrhosis must be managed appropriately. In some cases, surgical interventions such as transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPS), cholecystectomy, or liver transplantation may be required, particularly in patients with cirrhosis, cholestasis, or liver failure.
